package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	m := make(map[string]map[int]int)
	m["a"] = make(map[int]int)
	m["a"][1] = 8
	fmt.Println(m["a"][1])
}
What happens if you change a field on a copy of a struct taken from a map and do not write it back?
options: The map keeps the old struct; you mutated a copy
The map value updates because structs are references

questions.text: Why can two keys that store the same *T see each other’s field writes?
options: The map copies the struct into each key
Map values of pointer type share the pointed-to object

questions.text: If a callee does m = map[K]V{} on a map parameter, does the caller’s variable change?
options: Yes: the header is passed by reference
Yes if the map was empty
No. Rebinding the parameter copies a new header locally

questions.text: Is inserting a new key during range guaranteed to visit that key in the same loop?
options: It is unspecified: the new key may or may not be visited

questions.text: Can a slice type be used as a map key?
options: Yes if the slice is empty

questions.text: Can an array type be used as a map key?
options: Yes if the element type is comparable

questions.text: What is m["missing"] for m map[string]map[int]int?
A value receiver that assigns b.m[k] = v — does the caller’s map see it?
options: No. The whole map is copied
Yes. The header copy still points at the same table

questions.text: A value receiver that does b.m = newMap — does the caller’s field change?
options: No. Only the copy of the struct header is rebound

questions.text: Is deleting the current key during range specified as safe?
options: Yes. Remaining keys are still visited

questions.text: What is map[T]struct{} typically used as?
options: A set of T with empty values

questions.text: How are two struct keys compared in a map?
Why does m["a"]++ work for map[string]int?
options: The compiler rewrites it as a get, increment, and store
int values in maps are pointers

questions.text: After m2 := m1, a write to m2[k] — what does m1 see?
options: The old value: assignment clones the table
The new value: both headers share the table

questions.text: A map value of slice type: does mutating the original slice’s elements show up in the map?
options: No. The map stored a deep copy of the array
Only if you store a pointer to the slice
Yes. The stored slice header shares the backing array

questions.text: Two keys holding the same inner map — a write through one key?
options: The other key still sees the old inner map
Both keys see the write: the inner map is shared

questions.text: You can take the address of a map element with &m[k].
A range value variable is a copy, not an alias into the table.
Deleting every key during range is specified as safe.
make(map[int]int, 2) panics on the third insert.
A slice cannot be a map key.
An array of comparable elements can be a map key.
m1 == m2 compiles and compares contents.
A missing nested map reads as nil, not a panic.
A value receiver can still mutate map contents through a copied header.
A value receiver that replaces the map field updates the caller’s struct.
Stored false and a missing bool key both need comma-ok to tell apart.
m["a"]++ is illegal for map[string]int.
Assigning m2 := m1 clones all keys immediately.
map[T]struct{} is a common set idiom.
Struct keys compare by fields, not by variable identity.
Writing m[k].n = 9 compiles for map[K]Struct.
How do you update a struct stored in a map without using a pointer?
questions.answer: Copy it out, change the copy, assign it back.

questions.answer: The struct, including a copy of the map header.

questions.answer: A non-nil inner map at m[k].
